$$V_{out}\left[{1\over R_{D}}+{1\over R_{L}}+g_{ds}+g_{m}k\right]
=(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})V_{in}\tag{15}$$

Hence the exact small signal closed loop voltage gain

$${\cal A}_{f}\equiv {V_{out}\over V_{in}}
={g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}\over g_{ds}+R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{m}k}
={A_{0}\over 1+A_{0}\beta}\tag{16}$$

For $r_{o}\to \infty ,\;g_{mb}\to 0$

$${\cal A}_{f}={g_{m}\over R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{m}k}
={g_{m}R_{D}^{\prime}\over 1+g_{m}kR_{D}^{\prime}}
={A_{0}\over 1+T}\tag{16a}$$

$${\cal A}_{f}= {g_{m}R_{D}R_{L}\over R_{D}+R_{L}+g_{m}R_{D}R_{2}}
={g_{m}R_{D}(R_{1}+R_{2})\over R_{D}+R_{1}+R_{2}+g_{m}R_{D}R_{2}}\tag{16b}$$

In the high loop gain limit $T=g_{m}kR_{D}^{\prime}\gg 1$,

$${\cal A}_{f}\to {1\over \beta}={1\over k}=1+{R_{1}\over R_{2}}>0
\tag{17}$$

the familiar non inverting resistive gain, desensitised to
$g_{m},R_{D}$.  The condition is

$$g_{m}R_{D}{R_{2}\over R_{1}+R_{2}}\gg 1\qquad {\rm or}\qquad
g_{m}R_{D}^{\prime}\gg 1/k\tag{18}$$

For finite $T$

$${\cal A}_{f}={1\over \beta}{T\over 1+T}\tag{19}$$

Input resistance.  Let $I_{in}$ be the current forced into
the source terminal.  $I_{s}=I_{d}$,

$$I_{in}=-I_{s}=-I_{d}
=(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})V_{in}-g_{m}V_{F}-g_{ds}V_{out}\tag{20}$$

With $V_{out}={\cal A}_{f}V_{in}$ and $V_{F}=kV_{out}$,

$$I_{in}=V_{in}\left[(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})-{\cal A}_{f}(g_{m}k+g_{ds})\right]
=V_{in}(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}){R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}\over
R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}k}\tag{21}$$

so that

$$R_{if}\equiv {V_{in}\over I_{in}}
={R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}k\over
(g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds})(R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1})}
={1\over g_{m}+g_{mb}+g_{ds}}\left[1+{g_{m}k+g_{ds}\over
R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}}\right]\tag{22}$$

$$R_{if}=R_{i0}\,(1+T^{\prime})\qquad 
R_{i0}\approx {1\over g_{m}+g_{mb}}\tag{23}$$

with $T^{\prime}=g_{m}k/(R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds})$.
For $r_{o}\to\infty ,g_{mb}\to 0$,

$$R_{if}={1\over g_{m}}+k\,R_{D}^{\prime}
={1\over g_{m}}+{R_{2}\over R_{1}+R_{2}}\,R_{D}\parallel R_{L}
\tag{22a}$$

$$R_{if}\approx {1\over g_{m}}+R_{2}\parallel {R_{D}R_{2}\over R_{1}}
\approx {1\over g_{m}}+R_{2}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{D}\gg R_{L}\tag{22b}$$

$$R_{if}=R_{i0}(1+T)\tag{23a}$$

i. e. series mixing raises the low $1/g_{m}$ input resistance
of the common gate stage by $1+T$.  This is used to obtain
e. g. $50\,{\rm \Omega}$ wide band matching with

$$R_{if}=50\,{\rm \Omega}\approx {1\over g_{m}}+kR_{D}^{\prime}\tag{24}$$

without an inductor.

Output resistance.  Put $V_{in}=0$, apply $V_{x}$ at the
output, measure $I_{x}$.

$$V_{F}=kV_{x}\tag{25}$$
$$I_{d}=g_{m}kV_{x}+g_{ds}V_{x}\tag{26}$$
$$I_{x}={V_{x}\over R_{D}}+{V_{x}-V_{F}\over R_{1}}+I_{d}
=V_{x}\left[{1\over R_{D}}+{1\over R_{L}}+g_{ds}+g_{m}k\right]\tag{27}$$

Hence the resistance seen at the output node, $R_{D}$ and
$R_{L}$ included,

$$R_{of}\equiv {V_{x}\over I_{x}}
={1\over R_{D}^{-1}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}k}
={R_{o0}\over 1+T}\tag{28}$$

$$R_{o0}=R_{D}\parallel R_{L}\parallel r_{o}\tag{29}$$

The resistance seen looking into the drain alone is

$$R_{od}={1\over R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}k}\approx {1\over g_{m}k}
={R_{1}+R_{2}\over g_{m}R_{2}}\;\;{\rm for\;large\;}T\tag{30}$$

so that $R_{of}=R_{D}\parallel R_{od}$.  Voltage sampling
lowers the output resistance by $1+T$, improves drive
capability and extends bandwidth by the same factor,
$BW_{f}\approx BW_{0}(1+T)$.

In Blackman form $R_{of}=R_{o0}(1+T_{sc})/(1+T_{oc})$ with
$T_{oc}=T$, $T_{sc}=0$ for the $R_{D}$ inclusive port.

Remarks:

* $DC$ the divider provides self bias: $V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}$,
  $V_{F}=V_{out}R_{2}/(R_{1}+R_{2})$, $V_{GS}=V_{F}-V_{S}$,
  $V_{S}=V_{in,DC}$.  Saturation requires
  $V_{out}\ge V_{F}-V_{T}$ and $V_{DS}\ge V_{GS}-V_{T}$.

* For $T\gg 1$ the circuit is essentially an ideal
  non inverting voltage amplifier of gain $1+R_{1}/R_{2}$,
  input impedance $\approx (1+R_{1}/R_{2})/g_{m}$ and output
  impedance $\approx 0$, with all the usual feedback
  advantages: desensitivity, linearity, $BW$ extension,
  $R_{if}$ up, $R_{of}$ down.  With a single dominant pole
  at the output the resistive loop is unconditionally stable.

Any of (16), (22), (28) with $g_{mb}=0,\;r_{o}\to\infty$
is normally quoted as the ``resistive feedback common gate''
result, e. g.

$${\cal A}_{v}\approx {1+R_{1}/R_{2}\over 1+(1+R_{1}/R_{2})/g_{m}R_{D}}
\;\;,\;\;R_{in}\approx {1\over g_{m}}\left(1+g_{m}R_{D}{R_{2}\over
R_{1}+R_{2}}\right)\;\;,\;\;R_{out}\approx {R_{D}\over
1+g_{m}R_{D}R_{2}/(R_{1}+R_{2})}$$

which $\to 1+R_{1}/R_{2},\;R_{2}+1/g_{m},\; (R_{1}+R_{2})/g_{m}R_{2}$
for $g_{m}R_{D}\gg 1+R_{1}/R_{2}$.

answer.text:
With the usual low frequency $h_{\pi }=\infty $
model the forward amplifier is the $CG$ stage

$${\rm M}_{1}\;\;g_{m},g_{ds}=r_{o}^{-1}\;\;{\rm body\;to\;
source\;so\;}g_{mb}=0$$

$$V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{s}=V_{F}-V_{in}\qquad 
V_{ds}=V_{d}-V_{s}=V_{out}-V_{in}$$

$$I_{d}=g_{m}V_{gs}+g_{ds}V_{ds}
      =g_{m}(V_{F}-V_{in})+g_{ds}(V_{out}-V_{in})\tag{1}$$

directed from $D$ to $S$, i. e. out of the $V_{out}$
node into the device.

> {\it Topology :} $V_{out}$ is sampled by the
> divider $R_{1},R_{2}$ and the sample $V_{F}$ is
> subtracted in series from $V_{in}$ at the
> $V_{gs}$ port.  Voltage sampling, series mixing.
> In the conventional $series-shunt$ or $voltage-series$
> or $shunt-series$ nomenclature a $voltage-series$
> feedback amplifier.  Negative feedback: $V_{out}\uparrow
> \rightarrow V_{F}\uparrow \rightarrow V_{gs}\uparrow
> \rightarrow I_{d}\uparrow \rightarrow V_{out}=V_{DD}
> -I_{d}R_{D}\downarrow $.

For $I_{g}=0$

$$ \frac{V_{F}-V_{out}}{R_{1}}+\frac{V_{F}}{R_{2}}=0\tag{2}$$

$$V_{F}= \beta V_{out}\qquad 
\beta \equiv \frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}\tag{3}$$

is the {\it feedback factor}.  The ideal, $A\rightarrow \infty $,
closed loop gain is

$$V_{F}\approx V_{in}\;\;{\rm for\;large\;loop\;gain}$$

$$A_{id}= \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}\Biggr|_{id}= \frac{1}{\beta}
      =1+\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}>0\tag{4}$$

non inverting $CG$ gain.  The divider loads the output
with

$$R_{F}=R_{1}+R_{2}\tag{5}$$

to ac ground.  No loading at the input, $R_{iF}=\infty $.

KCL at the $V_{out}$ node, $V_{DD}$ ac ground,

$$\frac{V_{out}}{R_{D}}+\frac{V_{out}-V_{F}}{R_{1}}+I_{d}=0\tag{6}$$

with (1)(3)

$$\frac{V_{out}}{R_{D}}+\frac{V_{out}}{R_{F}}
      +g_{m}(\beta V_{out}-V_{in})+g_{ds}(V_{out}-V_{in})=0$$

$$\left[\frac{1}{R_{D}}+\frac{1}{R_{F}}+g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta \right]V_{out}
      =(g_{m}+g_{ds})V_{in}\tag{7}$$

$$\;A_{f}\equiv \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}
      =\frac{g_{m}+g_{ds}}{g_{ds}+R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta }\; \tag{8}$$

For $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty $

$$A_{f}= \frac{g_{m}}{R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta}
      =\frac{g_{m}R_{D}R_{F}}{R_{D}+R_{F}+g_{m}R_{D}R_{2}}\tag{9}$$

$$A_{f}= \frac{g_{m}R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o}}
            {1+g_{m}\beta \,R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o}}
            \times \frac{g_{m}+g_{ds}}{g_{m}}\approx 
            \frac{A_{0}}{1+\beta A_{0}} \tag{10}$$

where

$$A_{0}=g_{m}\,R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o}
      =\frac{g_{m}}{g_{ds}+R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}}\tag{11}$$

is the open loop $CG$ gain loaded by $R_{F}$ and

$$T\equiv \beta A_{0}= \frac{g_{m}\beta}{g_{ds}+R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}}
   =g_{m}\beta \,R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o}
   \approx g_{m}\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\tag{12}$$

is the loop gain, return ratio.  E. {\rm g}. breaking the
loop at the gate, $V_{in}=0$, $V_{t}$ injected at the gate,
$V_{d}=-g_{m}V_{t}R_{D}\parallel R_{F}$, $V_{r}=\beta V_{d}$,
$T=-V_{r}/V_{t}=g_{m}\beta R_{D}\parallel R_{F}$.  In the
usual $R_{F}\gg R_{D}$

$$T\approx g_{m}R_{D}\beta =g_{m}R_{D}\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}}\tag{13}$$

and

$$A_{f}= \frac{1}{\beta}\frac{T}{1+T}\xrightarrow[T\gg 1]{}\frac{1}{\beta}
      =1+\frac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}\tag{14}$$

the familiar desensitised gain.  E. {\rm g}. $g_{m}R_{D}=10$,
$R_{1}=9R_{2}$, $\beta =0.1$, $T\approx 1$, $A_{f}\approx 5$,
$T\gg 1$ requires $g_{m}R_{D}\gg 1/\beta$.

{\it Input impedance.}  Let $I_{in}$ be the current
injected into the source terminal.  $I_{in}=-I_{d}$,

$$I_{in}=-(g_{m}+g_{ds})V_{in}+(g_{m}\beta+g_{ds})V_{out}
      =V_{in}\left[(g_{m}+g_{ds})-(g_{m}\beta+g_{ds})A_{f}\right] \tag{15}$$

With (8)

$$Z_{in\,f}\equiv \frac{V_{in}}{I_{in}}
   =\frac{g_{ds}+R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta}
          {(g_{m}+g_{ds})(R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1})}\tag{16}$$

$$Z_{in\,f}= \frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{ds}}
            \left[1+\frac{g_{m}\beta+g_{ds}}{R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}}\right]
          =\frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{ds}}\left[1+T\frac{g_{m}\beta+g_{ds}}{g_{m}\beta}\right]$$

For $r_{o}\rightarrow \infty $

$$Z_{in\,f}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}+ \beta R_{D}\parallel R_{F}
            =\frac{1}{g_{m}}+\frac{R_{2}R_{D}}{R_{D}+R_{1}+R_{2}}\tag{17}$$

$$Z_{in\,0}= \frac{1+g_{ds}R_{D}\parallel R_{F}}{g_{m}+g_{ds}}
          \approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}\tag{18}$$

is the $CG$ impedance without feedback but loaded by $R_{F}$.
Hence

$$Z_{in\,f}\approx Z_{in\,0}(1+T)\;\;{\rm to\;within\;the\;
      loading\;factor\;}(1+R_{D}/R_{F})^{-1}$$

Series mixing raises the normally low $1/g_{m}$ input
impedance by $1+T$ to a value that can be made e. {\rm g}.
$50\,{\rm \Omega}$ for LNA matching: $Z_{in\,f}\approx
R_{2}$ for $R_{D}\gg R_{F}$ and $g_{m}R_{2}\gg 1$,
$Z_{in\,f}\approx R_{D}\parallel R_{2}$ for $R_{F}\gg R_{D}$.

{\it Output impedance.}  Put $V_{in}=0$, inject $V_{x}$ at
$V_{out}$, measure $I_{x}$.

$$I_{x}= \frac{V_{x}}{R_{D}}+\frac{V_{x}-V_{F}}{R_{1}}+I_{d}
     =V_{x}\left[\frac{1}{R_{D}}+\frac{1}{R_{F}}+g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta\right]\tag{19}$$

since $V_{F}=\beta V_{x}$ and $I_{d}=g_{m}\beta V_{x}+g_{ds}V_{x}$.

$$\;Z_{out\,f}\equiv \frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}
      =\frac{1}{g_{ds}+R_{D}^{-1}+R_{F}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta}
      =\frac{R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o}}{1+T}\; \tag{20}$$

including $R_{D}$.  Looking into the drain alone

$$Z_{d\,f}= \frac{1}{g_{ds}+R_{F}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta}
        =\frac{R_{F}\parallel r_{o}}{1+g_{m}\beta R_{F}\parallel r_{o}}\tag{21}$$

$$Z_{out\,0}=R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o}\tag{22}$$

so that

$$Z_{out\,f}= \frac{Z_{out\,0}}{1+T}\tag{23}$$

Voltage sampling lowers the output impedance by $1+T$.
For $T\gg 1$

$$Z_{out\,f}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}\beta}= \frac{R_{1}+R_{2}}{g_{m}R_{2}}
            \parallel R_{D}\parallel R_{F}\tag{24}$$

which can be a few $10\,{\rm \Omega}$.

In Blackman terms $Z_{in}$ sees series mixing,
$Z_{out}$ sees shunt sampling, as above.

DC bias, $M_{1}$ saturated:

$$I_{D}= \frac{V_{DD}-V_{OUT}}{R_{D}},\;\;
  V_{F}=V_{OUT}\frac{R_{2}}{R_{1}+R_{2}},\;\;
  V_{GS}=V_{F}-V_{IN}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2I_{D}/k_{n}},\;\;
  V_{DS}=V_{OUT}-V_{IN}>V_{GS}-V_{TH}$$

fixes $V_{IN},V_{OUT}$.  Body to source as drawn so no
$g_{mb}$; if body to ground replace $g_{m}\rightarrow
g_{m}+g_{mb}$ in $T$ and $Z_{in}$.

The circuit is a single pole loop and is unconditionally
stable; at high frequency $C_{gs},C_{gd},C_{db}$ add poles
in $A_{0}(s)$ and the usual $T(s)$ phase margin must be
checked.  Apart from that the resistive feedback makes the
closed loop gain essentially $1+R_{1}/R_{2}$, desensitised
to $g_{m},r_{o}$ and $R_{D}$, with raised $Z_{in}$ and
lowered $Z_{out}$, the classic series-shunt feedback
amplifier realized with a $CG$ forward stage.

answer.text:
This is the 1 transistor series-shunt
{\it voltage series} feedback amplifier.
In the conventional $shunt-series$ nomenclature
it is a shunt-shunt amplifier.

\begin{center}
{\it $M_{1}$ is a $CG$ voltage amplifier
$R_{1},R_{2}$ is the $\beta $ circuit}
\end{center}

$$V_{F}=\beta V_{out}\qquad 
\beta ={{V_{F}}\over {V_{out}}}{\Bigl |}_{I_{g}=0}$$

with the gate open $I_{g}=0$

$${{V_{F}}\over {V_{out}}}={{R_{2}}\over {R_{1}+R_{2}}}$$

in parallel with the output, in series with the
input at the source

$$\eqalign{
V_{gs}&=V_{g}-V_{s}=V_{F}-V_{in}\cr
V_{ds}&=V_{d}-V_{s}=V_{out}-V_{in}}$$

so that an increase of $V_{in}$ decreases $V_{gs}$,
decreases $I_{D}$, increases $V_{out}$, increases
$V_{F}$ and restores $V_{gs}$.  Negative feedback.
$V_{out}/V_{in}>0$, non inverting.

With $V_{DD}$ ac ground small signal

$$\eqalign{
I_{D}&=g_{m}V_{gs}+g_{ds}V_{ds}\cr
&=g_{m}(V_{g}-V_{s})+g_{ds}(V_{d}-V_{s})\cr
g_{ds}&=r_{o}^{-1}\cr
g_{m}^{\prime}&=g_{m}+g_{mb}{\rm \;if\;body\;effect}}$$

Put $V_{s}=V_{in}$, $V_{d}=V_{out}$, $V_{g}=V_{F}$.

KCL at $V_{out}$ and at $V_{F}$:

$$\eqalign{
{{V_{out}}\over {R_{D}}}+{{V_{out}-V_{F}}\over {R_{1}}}+I_{D}&=0\cr
{{V_{F}-V_{out}}\over {R_{1}}}+{{V_{F}}\over {R_{2}}}&=0\;\;I_{g}=0}$$

so that, as far as the gate loading is concerned,

$$V_{F}=V_{out}{{R_{2}}\over {R_{1}+R_{2}}}=\beta V_{out}\tag{1}$$

$${{V_{out}-V_{F}}\over {R_{1}}}={{V_{out}}\over {R_{1}+R_{2}}}\tag{2}$$

i. e. the feedback network loads the output with

$$R_{F}=R_{1}+R_{2}\tag{3}$$

to ac ground.  The $CG$ stage sees

$$R_{L}=R_{D}\parallel R_{F}=R_{D}\parallel (R_{1}+R_{2})\tag{4}$$

as drain load.  For $R_{F}\gg R_{D}$, $R_{L}\approx R_{D}$.
KCL at the drain with (1)(2):

$${{V_{out}}\over {R_{L}}}+g_{m}(\beta V_{out}-V_{in})
+g_{ds}(V_{out}-V_{in})=0$$

$${{V_{out}}\over {V_{in}}}=
{{g_{m}+g_{ds}}\over {g_{ds}+R_{L}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta}}\tag{5}$$

$$A_{v}\equiv {{V_{out}}\over {V_{in}}}=
{{g_{m}+g_{ds}}\over {R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}R_{2}/(R_{1}+R_{2})}}$$

For $r_{o}\to \infty $

$$A_{v}\approx {{g_{m}}\over {R_{L}^{-1}+g_{m}\beta}}
={1\over {\beta +1/g_{m}R_{L}}}={1\over \beta}
{1\over {1+1/g_{m}\beta R_{L}}}\tag{6}$$

The open circuit, loaded, $CG$ gain is

$$A_{0}=g_{m}R_{L}\parallel r_{o}\approx g_{m}R_{L}\tag{7}$$

and (6) is the familiar

$$A_{vf}={{A_{0}}\over {1+\beta A_{0}}}\tag{8}$$

apart from the $1+g_{ds}/g_{m}$ correction.
The loop or return ratio, breaking the loop at the
gate, $V_{s}=0$, $V_{g}=V_{t}$,

$$V_{d}=-g_{m}V_{t}\;R_{L}\parallel r_{o}\approx -g_{m}R_{L}V_{t}$$
$$V_{r}=\beta V_{d}$$

$$T\equiv -{{V_{r}}\over {V_{t}}}=g_{m}\beta R_{L}\parallel r_{o}
={{g_{m}\beta}\over {R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}}}\approx g_{m}\beta R_{L}\tag{9}$$

so that

$$A_{vf}={1\over \beta}{{T}\over {1+T}}\;{{1+g_{ds}/g_{m}}\over
{1+g_{ds}R_{L}/1+T}}\approx {1\over \beta}{{T}\over {1+T}}\tag{10}$$

For $T\gg 1$

$$A_{vf}^{id}={1\over \beta}={{R_{1}+R_{2}}\over {R_{2}}}=1+{{R_{1}}\over {R_{2}}}>0\tag{11}$$

exactly as a non inverting resistive op-amp.
The gain is stabilised against $g_{m},r_{o},R_{D},V_{DD},T$
to the ratio of two resistors.  In the usual design
$R_{F}\gg R_{D}$ and

$$A_{vf}\approx {{g_{m}R_{D}}\over {1+g_{m}R_{D}R_{2}/(R_{1}+R_{2})}}$$

$$T\approx g_{m}R_{D}{{R_{2}}\over {R_{1}+R_{2}}}$$

$T\gg 1$ requires $g_{m}R_{D}\gg 1+R_{1}/R_{2}$.

E. g. $R_{1}=9R_{2}$, $A_{vf}^{id}=10$, $T\approx 0.1g_{m}R_{D}$,
$g_{m}R_{D}>50$ for $1\%$ accuracy.

> {\it Remark:} With the usual $series-shunt$ two port
> decomposition the $A$ circuit is the $CG$ stage loaded at
> the output by $R_{1}+R_{2}$ and the $\beta $ circuit is
> (1).  Input loading of the $\beta $ circuit is nil,
> $I_{g}=0$, output loading is $R_{1}+R_{2}$.

Input resistance at the source.  With $V_{F}=\beta V_{out}$,
$V_{out}=A_{v}V_{in}$,

$$I_{in}=I_{s}= -I_{D}=g_{m}(V_{in}-V_{F})+g_{ds}(V_{in}-V_{out})$$

$$I_{in}=V_{in}(g_{m}+g_{ds})-V_{out}(g_{m}\beta+g_{ds})$$

$$I_{in}=V_{in}(g_{m}+g_{ds})\left[1-{{g_{m}\beta+g_{ds}}\over
{R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta}}\right]
=V_{in}(g_{m}+g_{ds}){{R_{L}^{-1}}\over {R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta}}$$

$$R_{if}\equiv {{V_{in}}\over {I_{in}}}=
{{R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta}\over {(g_{m}+g_{ds})R_{L}^{-1}}}
={{1+(g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta)R_{L}}\over {g_{m}+g_{ds}}}\tag{12}$$

$$R_{if}=R_{i0}(1+T)\tag{13}$$

where

$$R_{i0}={{1+g_{ds}R_{L}}\over {g_{m}+g_{ds}}}\approx {1\over g_{m}}\tag{14}$$

is the $CG$ input resistance with the gate ac ground
and drain load $R_{L}$.  For $r_{o}\to\infty$

$$R_{if}\approx {1\over g_{m}}+ \beta R_{L}
={1\over g_{m}}+{{R_{2}}\over {R_{1}+R_{2}}}R_{D}\parallel(R_{1}+R_{2})\tag{15}$$

$$R_{if}\approx {1\over g_{m}}+{{R_{D}R_{2}}\over {R_{D}+R_{1}+R_{2}}}$$

For $R_{D}\gg R_{F}$, $R_{L}\approx R_{F}$,

$$R_{if}\approx {1\over g_{m}}+R_{2}\tag{16}$$

The series mixing raises the normally low $1/g_{m}$
$CG$ input resistance by $1+T$.  It can be designed to
e. g. $50\,{\rm \Omega}$ wide band.

Output resistance at the drain.  Put $V_{in}=0$, apply
$V_{x}$ at $V_{out}$, $V_{F}=\beta V_{x}$,

$$I_{x}={{V_{x}}\over {R_{D}}}+{{V_{x}-V_{F}}\over {R_{1}}}
+g_{m}V_{F}+g_{ds}V_{x}$$

$$I_{x}=V_{x}\left[R_{L}^{-1}+g_{ds}+g_{m}\beta\right]\tag{17}$$

$$R_{of}\equiv {{V_{x}}\over {I_{x}}}=

This circuit is a **common-source amplifier with resistive feedback**, specifically using a **source degeneration resistor with feedback** (often called a "feedback resistor" or "source resistor" in this context, though it's not strictly degeneration in the classic sense due to the feedback path).

Let’s break down the circuit and analyze its operation:

---

### **1. Circuit Components**

- **M₁**: An NMOS transistor (enhancement mode, assuming standard symbol).
- **V_DD**: Supply voltage.
- **R_D**: Drain resistor (load resistor).
- **R_F**: Feedback resistor connected between the drain and the source of M₁.
- **R_S**: Source resistor (connected to ground).
- **V_in**: Input signal applied to the gate of M₁.
- **V_out**: Output signal taken from the drain of M₁.

---

### **2. Configuration: Common-Source with Feedback**

This is a **common-source amplifier** because:
- Input is at the **gate**.
- Output is at the **drain**.
- The **source** is not directly grounded — it’s connected to ground via R_S, and also connected to the drain via R_F → which introduces **negative feedback**.

The presence of **R_F** creates a **shunt-shunt (voltage-voltage) negative feedback** configuration:
- It samples the output voltage (at drain) and feeds back a current proportional to V_out to the source terminal.
- Since the source terminal is part of the input loop (along with gate), this feedback opposes the input signal → stabilizes gain, increases input/output impedance, reduces distortion.

---

### **3. DC Biasing Analysis (Qualitative)**

Assume the MOSFET is biased in saturation.

- The gate is biased by V_in (which may include a DC bias component).
- The source voltage is determined by the current through R_S and R_F.
- The drain voltage is V_DD - I_D * R_D.

Due to R_F, the source voltage is not just I_D * R_S — it’s also influenced by the feedback current from the drain.

In steady state (DC), we can write:

> V_GS = V_G - V_S  
> V_DS = V_D - V_S

But because of R_F, V_S is affected by V_D:

> V_S = I_S * R_S + I_F * R_F ≈ I_D * R_S + (V_D - V_S)/R_F * R_F  
> → V_S = I_D * R_S + (V_D - V_S)  
> → V_S = I_D * R_S + V_D - V_S  
> → 2V_S = I_D * R_S + V_D  
> → V_S = (I_D * R_S + V_D)/2

This shows that the source voltage is “pulled up” by the feedback, which affects V_GS and thus I_D.

---

### **4. Small-Signal AC Analysis**

We want to find the **voltage gain A_v = V_out / V_in**.

#### Step 1: Draw small-signal model

Replace M₁ with its small-signal model:
- Transconductance g_m
- Output resistance r_o (often neglected for simplicity if not given)
- Gate-source capacitances ignored for midband analysis

Resistors remain as is.

Feedback resistor R_F connects drain to source → so it forms a feedback path.

#### Step 2: Apply KCL at source node

Let’s define:
- v_gs = v_g - v_s
- i_d = g_m * v_gs (ignoring r_o for now)

At source node:

Current through R_S: i_s = v_s / R_S  
Current through R_F: i_f = (v_d - v_s) / R_F  
Total current into source: i_s + i_f = i_d (since all drain current flows out of source in small-signal)

So:

> i_d = v_s / R_S + (v_d - v_s) / R_F  
> g_m * (v_g - v_s) = v_s / R_S + (v_d - v_s) / R_F

Also, at drain node:

> v_d = -i_d * R_D  (because output is taken at drain, and current flows downward through R_D)

Substitute i_d = g_m*(v_g - v_s):

> v_d = -g_m * (v_g - v_s) * R_D

Now plug into the source equation:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) = v_s / R_S + [ -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D - v_s ] / R_F

Multiply both sides by R_F to eliminate denominator:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) R_F = (v_s R_F)/R_S + [ -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D - v_s ]

Bring all terms to one side:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) R_F + g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D + v_s = (v_s R_F)/R_S

Factor g_m (v_g - v_s):

> g_m (v_g - v_s) (R_F + R_D) + v_s = v_s R_F / R_S

Move v_s terms to left:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) (R_F + R_D) = v_s (R_F / R_S - 1)

Now solve for v_s:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) (R_F + R_D) = v_s (R_F / R_S - 1)

Expand left:

> g_m v_g (R_F + R_D) - g_m v_s (R_F + R_D) = v_s (R_F / R_S - 1)

Bring v_s terms together:

> g_m v_g (R_F + R_D) = v_s [ g_m (R_F + R_D) + (R_F / R_S - 1) ]

Thus:

> v_s = [ g_m (R_F + R_D) / ( g_m (R_F + R_D) + (R_F / R_S - 1) ) ] * v_g

Now recall:

> v_d = -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D

Substitute v_s:

Let’s denote:

> A = g_m (R_F + R_D)  
> B = R_F / R_S - 1  
> So v_s = [ A / (A + B) ] v_g

Then:

> v_g - v_s = v_g [ 1 - A/(A+B) ] = v_g [ B / (A + B) ]

So:

> v_d = -g_m * [ B / (A + B) ] * v_g * R_D

Thus, voltage gain:

> A_v = v_d / v_g = -g_m R_D * [ B / (A + B) ]

Substitute A and B:

> A_v = -g_m R_D * [ (R_F / R_S - 1) / ( g_m (R_F + R_D) + R_F / R_S - 1 ) ]

This expression is exact but messy. Often, we make approximations.

---

### **5. Approximation: If R_F >> R_S and g_m R_F >> 1**

If R_F is large compared to R_S, then R_F / R_S >> 1, and we can approximate:

> B ≈ R_F / R_S  
> A + B ≈ g_m (R_F + R_D) + R_F / R_S ≈ g_m R_F + R_F / R_S = R_F (g_m + 1/R_S)

Then:

> A_v ≈ -g_m R_D * [ (R_F / R_S) / ( R_F (g_m + 1/R_S) ) ]  
> = -g_m R_D * [ 1 / ( R_S (g_m + 1/R_S) ) ]  
> = -g_m R_D / ( g_m R_S + 1 )

Which simplifies to:

> **A_v ≈ - (g_m R_D) / (1 + g_m R_S)**

This is the familiar **gain formula for a common-source amplifier with source degeneration**.

But note: In our case, R_S is not purely degeneration — there’s also feedback via R_F. However, under the assumption that R_F is large and dominates, the circuit behaves like a degenerated CS amplifier.

---

### **6. Special Case: If R_S = 0**

If R_S = 0, then from earlier:

> A_v = -g_m R_D * [ (R_F / 0 - 1) / ... ] → undefined

Actually, if R_S = 0, then from source KCL:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) = (v_d - v_s)/R_F

And v_d = -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D

So:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) = [ -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D - v_s ] / R_F

Multiply both sides by R_F:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) R_F = -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D - v_s

Bring all to left:

> g_m (v_g - v_s) (R_F + R_D) + v_s = 0

> g_m v_g (R_F + R_D) - g_m v_s (R_F + R_D) + v_s = 0

> g_m v_g (R_F + R_D) = v_s [ g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1 ]

> v_s = [ g_m (R_F + R_D) / ( g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1 ) ] v_g

Then:

> v_d = -g_m (v_g - v_s) R_D

= -g_m R_D [ v_g - v_s ]

= -g_m R_D v_g [ 1 - g_m (R_F + R_D)/(g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1) ]

= -g_m R_D v_g [ (g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1 - g_m (R_F + R_D)) / (g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1) ]

= -g_m R_D v_g [ (-1) / (g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1) ]

So:

> **A_v = v_d / v_g = g_m R_D / (g_m (R_F + R_D) - 1)**

If g_m (R_F + R_D) >> 1, then:

> A_v ≈ R_D / (R_F + R_D)

This is interesting — the gain becomes approximately **R_D / (R_F + R_D)**, which is less than 1.

This makes sense: with R_S = 0, the feedback via R_F strongly attenuates the gain.

---

### **7. Summary of Key Points**

- This is a **common-source amplifier with negative feedback** via R_F.
- The feedback resistor R_F connects output (drain) to input (source), providing **voltage-voltage feedback**.
- The circuit has **stabilized gain**, **increased input/output impedance**, and **reduced distortion** compared to a simple CS amplifier.
- The voltage gain depends on g_m, R_D, R_S, and R_F.
- In practical design, R_F is often chosen to set the gain and stabilize the operating point.
- If R_S is present and R_F is large, the circuit approximates a **source-degenerated CS amplifier** with gain ≈ -g_m R_D / (1 + g_m R_S).
- If R_S = 0, gain becomes ≈ R_D / (R_F + R_D) when g_m is large.

---

### **8. Practical Use**

This topology is used in:
- Low-distortion amplifiers
- Stable gain stages where process variations must be compensated
- Op-amp input stages (though usually differential)

It’s a good example of how feedback can tame the high gain and variability of a single transistor stage.

---

✅ **Final Answer:**

The circuit is a **common-source MOSFET amplifier with resistive feedback** (via R_F). It provides **negative feedback** that stabilizes the gain, increases input/output impedance, and reduces distortion. The voltage gain is approximately:

> **A_v ≈ - \frac{g_m R_D}{1 + g_m R_S}**  (when R_F is large and R_S ≠ 0)

or

> **A_v ≈ \frac{R_D}{R_F + R_D}**  (when R_S = 0 and g_m is large)

depending on component values. The feedback resistor R_F plays a key role in determining the closed-loop gain and stability.

    Since the feedback voltage $V_F$ is in series with the input voltage $V_{in}$ (they subtract to determine $V_{GS}$), this is **series mixing** (or series feedback at the input).

## Circuit identification

* **M1** is an **NMOS** transistor. The arrow on the lower lead marks the **source**, so the source is tied to the input terminal $V_{in}$, the **drain** is tied to the output node $V_{out}$, and the **gate** is driven by the node $V_F$.
* $R_D$ is the drain load to $V_{DD}$.
* $R_1$–$R_2$ form a resistive voltage divider from $V_{out}$ to ground; the gate (no DC current) sits at the divider midpoint $V_F$.

So the input signal is injected at the **source** and the feedback signal is injected at the **gate** – the two signals combine in series around the gate–source loop ($V_{GS}=V_F-V_{in}$). This is the "source‑input, resistive‑feedback" topology.

## Feedback topology

| Aspect | Observation | Type |
|---|---|---|
| Output sampling | $R_1$–$R_2$ is connected in parallel with the output and senses $V_{out}$ | **Voltage (shunt)** |
| Input mixing | $V_{in}$ (source) and $V_F$ (gate) add in series in the $V_{GS}$ loop | **Series** |

Hence the circuit is a **voltage–series (series–shunt) feedback amplifier**, i.e. a **non‑inverting voltage amplifier**.

## Small‑signal model

Let $g_m$ be the transconductance and $r_o$ the output resistance of M1. Define

$$\beta = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}, \qquad R_L = R_D \parallel (R_1+R_2)$$

(The divider draws $V_{out}/(R_1+R_2)$ from the output node, so it loads the output as $R_1+R_2$.)

With $v_f=\beta\,v_{out}$ and $v_{gs}=v_f-v_{in}=\beta v_{out}-v_{in}$, KCL at the output node gives

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}+\frac{v_{out}-v_f}{R_1}+g_m(\beta v_{out}-v_{in})=0$$

which reduces to

$$\boxed{\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_m\,R_L}{1+g_m\beta R_L}\,}$$

This is exactly the series–shunt form $A_v=A/(1+AF)$ with

* open‑loop gain $A = g_m R_L$ (gain from source to drain with the gate at a.c. ground),
* feedback factor $F = \beta$,
* **loop gain** $T = AF = g_m\,\beta\,R_L = g_m\,R_2\,R_L/(R_1+R_2)$.

Because $A_v>0$, the amplifier is **non‑inverting**. For $T\gg 1$:

$$A_v \;\xrightarrow{T\gg1}\; \frac{1}{\beta} = 1+\frac{R_1}{R_2}$$

i.e. the closed‑loop gain is set almost entirely by the resistive divider, just like a non‑inverting op‑amp stage.

## Effect of feedback on the impedances

* **Input resistance** (looking into the source). The basic resistance looking into the source is $1/g_m$; series feedback multiplies it by $(1+T)$:

$$R_{in}=\frac{1}{g_m}(1+T)=\frac{1}{g_m}+\beta R_L$$

* **Output resistance** (looking into $V_{out}$). The basic output resistance is $R_L\parallel r_o$; shunt (voltage) sampling divides it by $(1+T)$:

$$R_{out}=\frac{R_L\parallel r_o}{1+T}\;\xrightarrow{T\gg1}\;\frac{1}{g_m\beta}$$

So the feedback **raises** the input resistance and **lowers** the output resistance, as expected for a series–shunt (voltage) feedback amplifier.

## Operating‑region note

With the source at the input (≈ 0 V d.c. for a zero‑bias source), the gate d.c. level is $V_{G}=V_{out}\,R_2/(R_1+R_2)$, set self‑consistently by the divider. The device is in saturation provided $V_{GS}=V_G-V_S>V_{th}$, which the bias point satisfies; $R_D$ then supplies the drain current and, together with the divider, fixes $R_L$ and hence the loop gain.

### Summary
Figure 9 is a **non‑inverting voltage amplifier** realized with a single NMOS and a resistive divider, using **voltage‑series (series–shunt) feedback** with the input applied at the source. Its closed‑loop gain is $A_v=g_mR_L/(1+g_m\beta R_L)\approx 1+R_1/R_2$, its input resistance is boosted to $(1/g_m)(1+T)$, and its output resistance is reduced to $(R_L\parallel r_o)/(1+T)$.

M₁ is wired as a **common‑gate / source‑input** stage:

* **Source** ← input terminal $V_{in}$
* **Drain** ← output node $V_{out}$ (pulled up to $V_{DD}$ through $R_D$)
* **Gate** ← feedback node $V_F$

The pair $R_1$–$R_2$ is a voltage divider from $V_{out}$ to ground. Because the MOSFET gate draws no current,

$$V_F = \beta\,V_{out},\qquad \beta = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$$

so the output **voltage** is sampled (shunt/voltage sampling) and returned to the gate, where it appears **in series** with $V_{in}$ around the gate–source loop ($v_{GS}=v_F-v_{in}$). Hence the topology is **series–shunt (voltage–series) negative feedback**, i.e. a voltage amplifier.

## Small‑signal closed‑loop gain

Let $v_s=v_{in}$, $v_d=v_{out}$, $v_g=\beta v_{out}$, so $v_{GS}=\beta v_{out}-v_{in}$. KCL at the drain node (currents leaving = 0), including $r_o$:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}+\frac{v_{out}-v_F}{R_1}+g_m v_{GS}+\frac{v_{out}-v_s}{r_o}=0$$

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_D}+\frac{(1-\beta)v_{out}}{R_1}+g_m(\beta v_{out}-v_{in})+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_o}=0$$

Collecting terms:

$$\boxed{\,A_{cl}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o}}{\dfrac{1}{R_D}+\dfrac{1-\beta}{R_1}+\beta g_m+\dfrac{1}{r_o}}\,}$$

Using $\dfrac{1-\beta}{R_1}=\dfrac{1}{R_1+R_2}$, the denominator is $G_L+\beta g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o}$ with $G_L=\tfrac{1}{R_D}+\tfrac{1}{R_1+R_2}$.

* **High loop gain** ($\beta g_m \gg G_L+\tfrac{1}{r_o}$): $\;A_{cl}\to \dfrac{1}{\beta}=\dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_2}$  (the familiar non‑inverting value).
* **Check – no feedback** ($\beta=0$): $A_{cl}=(g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o})(R_D\|R_1\|r_o)$, the ordinary common‑gate gain. ✓

The loop gain is $T\approx g_m\,\beta\,(R_D\|(R_1+R_2))$, so the closed‑loop gain is $A'/(1+T)$ with $A'=g_m(R_D\|(R_1+R_2))$.

## Input and output resistances

**Output resistance** (set $V_{in}=0$, test at $V_{out}$): the gate sees $\beta v_t$, so

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{R_D}+\dfrac{1}{R_1+R_2}+\beta g_m+\dfrac{1}{r_o}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\beta g_m}\quad(\text{large }g_m)$$

i.e. the voltage feedback **lowers** $R_{out}$ to $\approx 1/(\beta g_m)$.

**Input resistance** (look into the source terminal):

$$R_{in}=\frac{1}{g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o}-A_{cl}\!\left(\beta g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o}\right)}=\frac{G_L+\beta g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o}}{\left(g_m+\tfrac{1}{r_o}\right)G_L}\;\approx\;\frac{\beta}{G_L}=\beta\!\left(R_D\|(R_1+R_2)\right)$$

Note that, because the signal is injected at the **source** (common‑gate), the input resistance stays low (order $1/g_m$ without feedback, $\beta R_L$ with feedback); the series feedback boosts the resistance seen at the *gate*, not at the source terminal.

## Summary

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| Feedback type | series–shunt (voltage–series), negative |
| Closed‑loop gain (exact) | $\dfrac{g_m+1/r_o}{1/R_D+1/(R_1+R_2)+\beta g_m+1/r_o}$ |
| Closed‑loop gain (ideal) | $\dfrac{R_1+R_2}{R_2}$ |
| $R_{out}$ | $\approx 1/(\beta g_m)$ |
| $R_{in}$ | $\approx \beta\,[R_D\|(R_1+R_2)]$ |

So the circuit is a resistively‑fed, source‑driven MOSFET amplifier whose closed‑loop voltage gain is set by the $R_1$–$R_2$ divider, tending to $(R_1+R_2)/R_2$ when the loop gain is large.

To analyze the given common-source (CS) MOSFET amplifier with **local negative voltage feedback**, we break down the analysis into DC biasing, small-signal performance (gain, input/output resistance), feedback type, and special cases:
---
## 1. Circuit Overview
The circuit uses an nMOSFET \(M_1\) in a common-source configuration:
- Input is applied to the **gate** (\(V_{in}\)), output is taken from the **drain** (\(V_{out}\)).
- A resistive feedback network (\(R_1, R_2\)) senses the drain (output) voltage and feeds back a fraction to the MOSFET **source**, providing negative feedback.
- \(R_D\) is the drain load resistor, connected to \(V_{DD}\).
---
## 2. DC Biasing Analysis
For the MOSFET to operate in the **saturation region** (active amplification mode):
1.  The DC drain current \(I_D\) flows through \(R_D\), so the DC drain voltage is:
    \[
    V_{out,DC} = V_{DD} - I_D R_D
    \]
2.  All drain current flows through \(R_1\) to the source, then through \(R_2\) to ground, so the DC source voltage is:
    \[
    V_{F,DC} = I_D R_2
    \]
3.  The gate DC bias \(V_{in,DC}\) sets the gate-source voltage \(V_{GS} = V_{in,DC} - V_{F,DC}\). The saturation condition requires:
    \[
    V_{DS} = V_{out,DC} - V_{F,DC} = V_{DD} - I_D(R_D + R_2) \geq V_{GS} - V_{th}
    \]
    where \(V_{th}\) is the MOSFET threshold voltage, and \(I_D = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS} - V_{th})^2\) for long-channel operation (ignoring channel length modulation initially).
---
## 3. Small-Signal Analysis
We use the MOSFET small-signal model: transconductance \(g_m\) (controlled current source \(g_m v_{gs}\) from drain to source) and output resistance \(r_o\) (due to channel length modulation, from drain to source). The gate draws no input current (high impedance).
### a. Voltage Gain \(A_v = v_{out}/v_{in}\)
Using KCL at the drain and source nodes, and solving the resulting linear system (or using feedback theory), the general gain (including \(r_o\)) is:
\[
\boldsymbol{A_v = \frac{ - g_m R_D R_1 (r_o - R_2) }{ r_o\left(R_D + R_1 + R_2 + g_m R_1 R_2\right) + R_D R_1 (1 + g_m R_2) }}
\]
For the common approximation \(r_o \to \infty\) (large output resistance, valid for long-channel MOSFETs), this simplifies to:
\[
\boldsymbol{A_v \approx \frac{ - g_m R_D R_1 }{ R_D + R_1 + R_2 + g_m R_1 R_2 } = \frac{ - g_m R_D }{ 1 + g_m R_2 + \frac{R_D + R_2}{R_1} }}
\]
- The negative sign indicates a **180° phase shift** (inverting operation), standard for CS amplifiers.
- The magnitude of the gain is reduced by negative feedback, compared to the open-loop CS gain (no feedback, \(R_2=0\)): \(A_{ol} = -g_m(R_D || R_1 || r_o)\).
---
### b. Input Resistance \(R_{in}\)
The input is applied to the insulated MOSFET gate, which draws negligible current (\(i_{in} \approx 0\)). Series feedback further increases input resistance, so:
\[
\boldsymbol{R_{in} \to \infty}
\]
This high input resistance makes the stage suitable for voltage input signals, with no loading of the preceding circuit.
---
### c. Output Resistance \(R_{out}\)
Found by setting \(v_{in}=0\) and applying a test voltage at the output, the output resistance is:
\[
\boldsymbol{R_{out} = \frac{ R_D R_2 \left(g_m + \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{r_o}\right) }{ R_2\left(g_m + \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{r_o}\right) + (R_D + R_2)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{r_o}\right) }}
\]
For \(r_o \to \infty\):
\[
R_{out} \approx \frac{ R_D R_2 \left(g_m + \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\right) }{ R_2\left(g_m + \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\right) + \frac{R_D + R_2}{R_1} }
\]
Shunt (voltage) feedback reduces the output resistance below the open-loop value \(R_{out,ol} = R_D || r_o\), as expected for negative feedback, making the stage better at driving voltage loads.
---
## 4. Feedback Type
This is **voltage-series (series-shunt) negative feedback**:
1.  **Series mixing**: The feedback voltage \(v_f\) (from the R1-R2 divider) is *subtracted* from the input voltage to produce \(v_{gs} = v_{in} - v_f\), so it is series feedback at the input.
2.  **Voltage sampling**: The feedback network senses the output *voltage* \(v_{out}\), so it is shunt sampling at the output.
3.  **Negative feedback**: The feedback signal reduces the effective \(v_{gs}\), stabilizing the gain, improving linearity, reducing distortion, and increasing bandwidth relative to the open-loop CS stage.
---
## 5. Special Cases
1.  **\(R_2 = 0\) (no feedback, source grounded)**: The circuit reduces to a standard CS amplifier with load \(R_D || R_1 || r_o\), with gain \(A_v = -g_m(R_D || R_1 || r_o)\), as expected.
2.  **\(R_1 \to \infty\) (source degeneration)**: The feedback network reduces to only \(R_2\), giving source degeneration, with gain:
    \[
    A_v \approx \frac{ -g_m R_D }{ 1 + g_m R_2 + \frac{R_D + R_2}{r_o} }
    \]
    This linearizes the amplifier, reduces gain, and increases input resistance (though input resistance is already very high for MOSFETs).
3.  **Large \(g_m\) (strong MOSFET)**: The gain simplifies to \(A_v \approx -R_D/R_2\), as the high transconductance makes the source voltage follow the input, so the gain is set by the \(R_D/R_2\) ratio.
---
## Final Notes
This circuit is a high-input-impedance inverting voltage amplifier, with gain stabilized by local negative feedback, suitable for low-frequency voltage signal applications. The feedback reduces gain but improves linearity and bandwidth, typical of feedback amplifier design.

This circuit uses **negative voltage-series (series-shunt) feedback**:
1.  **Sampling**: The output *voltage* is sampled (shunt sampling) by the $R_1$-$R_2$ divider.
2.  **Mixing**: The feedback voltage $v_f$ is applied *in series* with the input, subtracting from $v_{in}$ to set $v_{gs} = v_{in} - v_f$.
3.  **Effect of Feedback**:

Including the MOSFET output resistance $r_o$ (between drain and source) slightly increases the gain and output resistance:

answer.text:
To analyze the circuit, we first identify it as an **n-channel common-source MOSFET amplifier with positive voltage feedback**, implemented via resistors $R_1$ (drain-to-source) and $R_2$ (source-to-ground). Below is the full analysis:
---
## 1. Circuit & Feedback Identification
- $M_1$ is an nMOSFET: input at the gate ($V_{in}$), output at the drain ($V_{out}$), source connected to the feedback network at $V_F$.
- $R_D$ is the drain load resistor, connected to $V_{DD}$.
- The feedback network $R_1, R_2$ samples the **output voltage** ($V_{out}$, shunt sampling) and feeds back a voltage $V_F$ to the source, which is subtracted from the input voltage at the gate (series mixing). This is **voltage-series (series-shunt) positive feedback** (regenerative feedback).
---
## 2. DC Bias Analysis
From KCL at the drain and source nodes, and the MOSFET DC current relation ($I_D = K(V_{GS}-V_{th})^2$ for saturation, $K = \frac{1}{2}\mu_n C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}$):
1.  KCL at the drain node: $I_{RD} + I_D = I_{R1}$, where $I_{RD} = \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_D}$ (current through $R_D$), $I_{R1} = \frac{V_{out}-V_F}{R_1}$ (current through $R_1$).
2.  KCL at the source node: $I_{R1} = I_D + I_{R2}$, where $I_{R2} = \frac{V_F}{R_2}$ (current through $R_2$).
Adding these two equations cancels $I_{R1}$ and $I_D$, giving the key DC relation:
$$\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_D} = \frac{V_F}{R_2} \implies V_{out} = V_{DD} - \frac{R_D}{R_2}V_F$$
The drain current is also:
$$I_D = \frac{V_{out}-V_F}{R_1} - \frac{V_F}{R_2}$$
For saturation region operation, $V_{DS} = V_{out}-V_F \ge V_{GS} - V_{th} = (V_{in} - V_F) - V_{th}$.
---
## 3. Small-Signal Analysis
We use the small-signal MOSFET model: $i_d = g_m v_{gs}$ (ignore output conductance $r_o$ for simplicity, $g_m$ = transconductance, $v_{gs} = v_{in} - v_F$), with $V_{DD}$ as AC ground.
### 3.1 Small-Signal KCL
1.  **Drain node**: Currents into the drain: $i_{RD} = \frac{0 - v_{out}}{R_D}$ (from $R_D$) and $i_d$ (from MOSFET). Current out: $i_{R1} = \frac{v_{out}-v_F}{R_1}$. KCL gives:
    $$-\frac{v_{out}}{R_D} + i_d = \frac{v_{out}-v_F}{R_1} \tag{1}$$
2.  **Source node**: Current into $V_F$: $i_{R1}$ (from $R_1$) and $i_s = i_d$ (source current, equal to $i_d$ for MOSFET). Current out: $i_{R2} = \frac{v_F}{R_2}$. KCL gives:
    $$\frac{v_{out}-v_F}{R_1} + i_d = \frac{v_F}{R_2} \tag{2}$$
3.  MOSFET small-signal current: $i_d = g_m(v_{in} - v_F) \tag{3}$
### 3.2 Solve for Gain
From the DC bias relation, the small-signal variations satisfy $\Delta I_{RD} = \Delta I_{R2}$, so:
$$i_{RD} = i_{R2} \implies -\frac{v_{out}}{R_D} = \frac{v_F}{R_2} \implies v_{out} = -\frac{R_D}{R_2}v_F \tag{4}$$
Substitute (3) and (4) into (2), and simplify to solve for $v_F$ in terms of $v_{in}$, then substitute back to find $v_{out}/v_{in}$:
$$\boldsymbol{A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = \frac{g_m R_1 R_D}{R_1 + R_2 + R_D - g_m R_1 R_2}}$$
#### Gain Behavior:
- For $g_m R_1 R_2 < R_1 + R_2 + R_D$: Denominator positive, $A_v > 0$ (non-inverting, positive feedback, stable operation, gain magnitude < 1 for typical values).
- For $g_m R_1 R_2 = R_1 + R_2 + R_D$: Denominator = 0, gain is infinite (circuit acts as a regenerative latch, unstable).
- For $g_m R_1 R_2 > R_1 + R_2 + R_D$: Denominator negative, DC bias shifts to $M_1$ off ($V_{out}=V_{DD}, V_F=0$), latching behavior.
---
## 4. Input/Output Impedance
### 4.1 Input Impedance ($Z_{in}$)
The MOSFET gate draws no DC or small-signal current, so $Z_{in}$ is **infinite** (open circuit) for an ideal MOSFET. The series feedback further increases input impedance, but it remains infinite for practical purposes.
### 4.2 Output Impedance ($Z_{out}$)
Set $v_{in}=0$ (gate grounded), apply a test voltage $v_{test}$ at $V_{out}$, and solve for the drawn current $i_{test}$:
$$Z_{out} = R_D \parallel \left(R_1 + R_2 - g_m R_1 R_2\right) = \frac{R_D\left(R_1 + R_2 - g_m R_1 R_2\right)}{R_D + R_1 + R_2 - g_m R_1 R_2}$$
#### Output Impedance Behavior:
- For $g_m R_1 R_2 < R_1 + R_2$: $Z_{out}$ is positive, less than $R_D$.
- For $g_m R_1 R_2 = R_1 + R_2$: $Z_{out}$ is infinite (open circuit).
- For $g_m R_1 R_2 > R_1 + R_2$: $Z_{out}$ is negative, a signature of positive feedback, meaning the circuit can supply power to the load (active impedance).
---
## 5. Key Notes
- The positive feedback arises because an increase in $V_{out}$ reduces $V_F$ (via $I_{RD}=I_{R2}$), increasing $V_{GS}$, which increases $I_D$, further increasing $V_{out}$.
- The circuit operates as a low-gain, non-inverting amplifier for stable operating points, or as a latch when the loop gain reaches 1.
- For standard negative feedback, the feedback connection would be reversed (source to ground, feedback from drain to gate), but this configuration uses positive feedback for regenerative operation.
